paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning combines a policy that chooses actions with a critic that evaluates them. This paper addresses whether that combination can learn efficiently when an agent must deliberately explore and uses general function approximation. Its central contribution is an algorithm with an inverse-square dependence on the desired policy accuracy in its trajectory requirement.

The algorithm combines optimism, critic estimation from off-policy data aimed at the optimal action-value function, and occasional policy resets. Its sample bound also depends on the Bellman eluder dimension, the decision horizon, and the sizes of the action space and critic function class. The accompanying square-root-in-time regret result requires that the Bellman eluder dimension grow no faster than logarithmically with time.

The authors also study hybrid reinforcement learning, which combines offline data with further interaction. Initializing the critic using offline data improves sample efficiency in their analysis, and they provide a provably efficient non-optimistic actor-critic algorithm for that setting. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The results establish efficiency guarantees for these particular algorithmic designs and conditions.
icml-2025-actor-critics-can-achieve-opti.tldr: A new actor-critic algorithm achieves inverse-square accuracy dependence in sample complexity, with conditional regret guarantees and extensions that benefit from offline data.

paragraphs: Language models can represent the meanings of medical concepts in electronic health records, but those meanings do not fully capture how concepts are organized. Medical concepts also belong to hierarchies, including relationships supplied by domain knowledge. BoxLM brings these structural relationships into the same framework as language-based representations for diagnosis prediction.

The framework uses box embeddings to combine hierarchies derived from medical ontologies and patient records with semantic embeddings from a language model. This fusion produces interpretable concept representations. A separate patient-modeling mechanism updates and retains information across visits, allowing the patient representation to reflect changes over time. Diagnosis prediction then uses a similarity measure based on box volumes.

The reported experiments show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with particularly strong results when few training examples are available. These findings support combining the organization of medical knowledge with its textual meaning, while also accounting for a patient's visit history. The demonstrated outcome is improved diagnosis prediction in the experiments, which the authors present as evidence of potential practical clinical utility.
icml-2025-boxlm-unifying-structures-and-.tldr: BoxLM combines medical hierarchies, language-based meaning, and changing patient histories through box embeddings to improve diagnosis prediction.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning describes an example through the relative contributions of several labels. The paper argues that these proportions leave out absolute intensity: they describe how the represented labels compare without fully describing how strongly those labels characterize the example. Information associated with labels outside the available label space is also missing, which can make instances harder to distinguish.

The authors introduce background concentration as an additional quantity representing absolute description degree. Combining it with the usual label distribution produces their concentration distribution learning framework. Their model brings together probabilistic methods and neural networks to learn both quantities from existing label distribution datasets. This makes the additional concentration information something the model infers alongside its label predictions.

Experiments report that the approach can extract background concentrations from label distributions and achieve more accurate predictions than state-of-the-art label distribution learning methods. The contribution is therefore both representational and predictive: it adds an intensity-related component to relative label descriptions, and the reported comparisons show that learning this component can improve prediction.
icml-2025-concentration-distribution-lea.tldr: The paper augments relative label distributions with a learned background concentration to capture absolute intensity and improve prediction.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations encode data in the parameters of a network that represents a continuous function. Generating new data therefore involves learning how such network parameters vary. The paper argues that describing all parameter variation through one flat latent vector can obscure the hierarchy across network layers, mixing semantic factors together and making generation difficult to control.

CHINR explicitly models this hierarchy in two stages. First, a Layers-of-Experts network gives each layer its own latent vector so that different layers can modulate distinct semantics. Second, a Hierarchical Conditional Diffusion Model learns dependencies between these layers. The second stage accounts for how choices at different levels relate, supporting generation with control at multiple semantic granularities.

Experiments across different modalities report improved generalizability and flexible hierarchical control over generated content. The stated findings support organizing the generative representation around layer-dependent structure. The approach matters because it links the organization of the parameter space to the user's ability to control different aspects of generated data, while still modeling dependencies among those aspects.
icml-2025-controllable-data-generation-w.tldr: CHINR models dependencies across neural representation layers to improve generalization and enable generation controlled at different semantic levels.

paragraphs: Computer agents often encounter environments with separately designed observation and action interfaces. The paper identifies these differences as a major obstacle to generalization. It proposes General Computer Control, a setting in which the agent sees screenshots and acts through the keyboard and mouse. This supplies a common interaction interface across software.

Cradle is a preliminary framework for this setting, powered by a large multimodal model. Its six modules handle information gathering, self-reflection, task inference, skill curation, action planning, and memory. Together, they connect visual observations and high-level planning to executable code for low-level input control. The framework is designed to carry out complex, extended tasks without relying on software-specific built-in APIs.

Experiments cover four commercial games, five software applications, and the OSWorld benchmark. The authors report strong performance and generalization across these environments. The significance is the breadth achievable through one interface: the same screenshot-and-input arrangement supports interaction with varied software. These results present Cradle as a step toward general computer agents, with the framework's general-purpose interface demonstrated across the tested settings.
icml-2025-cradle-empowering-foundation-a.tldr: Cradle combines multimodal reasoning, planning, and memory to operate varied software through screenshots and keyboard-and-mouse actions.

paragraphs: Federated active learning aims to train a shared model while requesting as few labels as possible. Selecting useful examples across clients is difficult when privacy requirements prevent access to cross-client query information. FALE addresses this problem for regression tasks in which clients have different data distributions, so local selection decisions must account for a heterogeneous overall dataset.

The method builds on FedSVD to estimate the usefulness of unlabeled examples and select them through leverage score sampling. Its design lets the server coordinate global selection in a privacy-preserving way. The authors also introduce a secure regression-learning framework to use the resulting supervision. FALE needs no initially labeled dataset and selects examples in one pass, reducing communication overhead.

The theoretical analysis establishes label-query requirements for constant-factor and relative-error approximation guarantees. Experiments on 11 benchmark datasets report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. The combined contribution is a selection procedure with approximation analysis and a practical communication advantage, developed specifically for federated regression with non-identically distributed client data.
icml-2025-efficient-heterogeneity-aware-.tldr: FALE uses leverage score sampling to select useful regression labels across heterogeneous clients in a single privacy-preserving pass.

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning asks multiple clients to build a shared model with only one communication round with a central server. FedBEns approaches this problem through Bayesian inference. Its central idea is that a client's local learning problem can have multiple promising solutions, and the information sent to the server should preserve that variety.

The method represents each client's local posterior using a mixture of Laplace approximations. Each approximation captures a local region, while the mixture represents multiple regions together. The server aggregates these local posterior representations to infer a global model. This makes multimodality—the presence of multiple distinct possibilities—a feature used in aggregation, rather than reducing each client's contribution to a single mode.

Experiments across various datasets show FedBEns outperforming competing baselines that typically use unimodal local approximations. The finding supports retaining multiple local possibilities when forming a global model under a strict communication constraint. Its significance is specifically tied to the one-shot setting: the richer posterior representation helps the server combine client information within the single available round.
icml-2025-fedbens-one-shot-federated-lea.tldr: FedBEns improves one-shot federated learning by combining Bayesian representations that preserve multiple promising solutions at each client.

paragraphs: A diffusion model's generated samples may need to satisfy an additional objective, such as greater image darkness or improved aesthetics. This paper studies alignment with a continuous reward function that expresses such an objective. Direct Noise Optimization, or DNO, adjusts the noise injected during sampling so that generation favors higher-reward outputs.

Because the optimization happens during generation, DNO does not require tuning the pretrained model and is prompt-agnostic. The authors analyze its theoretical properties and develop variants for rewards that are not differentiable. This makes the sampling process itself the point of control: alignment proceeds online as outputs are generated, using the reward to guide noise optimization.

The paper also identifies a concrete failure mode. Naive DNO can produce high-reward samples outside the support of the pretrained distribution, an instance of reward hacking. The authors introduce probability regularization informed by high-dimensional statistics to address this issue. Experiments across several reward functions report state-of-the-art reward scores within a reasonable generation-time budget, supporting the approach while motivating its distribution-aware regularization.
icml-2025-inference-time-alignment-of-di.tldr: DNO steers diffusion outputs by optimizing sampling noise at inference time, with probability regularization to address out-of-distribution reward hacking.

paragraphs: The Hessian describes the curvature of a model's training loss around its parameters. Earlier accounts emphasized a few large eigenvalues alongside many values close to zero. This paper reports a more detailed power-law pattern in well-trained networks, including convolutional networks and large language models. It examines what that pattern reveals about learning behavior.

The authors give a maximum-entropy interpretation of the observed structure and theoretically establish the existence of a robust, low-dimensional subspace in deep networks. They also introduce a spectral method based on the power-law pattern. Their experiments connect the Hessian spectrum to optimization, generalization, and overparameterization, giving the proposed structure relevance beyond a descriptive account of curvature.

A particularly consequential finding concerns language models: the power-law structure of a given model can predict generalization during training. In the reported investigation, conventional sharpness-based measures that often work for convolutional networks are nearly uninformative for this purpose in language models. The findings support examining richer spectral structure when assessing generalization, especially when familiar curvature summaries do not transfer well across model families.
icml-2025-investigating-the-overlooked-h.tldr: The paper identifies power-law Hessian structure in trained networks and finds it useful for predicting language-model generalization during training.

paragraphs: Some prediction tasks require outputs to change monotonically with inputs, preserving a specified direction of change. Traditional approaches enforce this through model construction or regularization. This paper offers another formulation for strictly monotonic probabilities: view them through an ordering relationship between an observed revenue variable and an unobserved cost variable.

With that formulation, the learning problem becomes modeling the latent cost. The proposed Generative Cost Model uses a generative network for this variable and inherently handles the strict monotonicity problem. The authors also introduce an Implicit Generative Cost Model for implicit monotonic relationships. The shared idea is to express the desired probability behavior through a model of the hidden cost rather than treating monotonicity solely as an added constraint.

The evaluation includes a numerical quantile-regression simulation and experiments on public datasets. The authors report significant improvements over existing monotonic modeling techniques. These findings support latent-cost modeling as a useful route to monotonic prediction, with separate proposed models addressing the strict and implicit versions of the problem.
icml-2025-learning-monotonic-probabiliti.tldr: The paper learns monotonic probabilities by modeling a latent cost variable, with separate generative models for strict and implicit monotonicity.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can supply prior information about plausible signals when recovering them from measurements. This paper targets nonlinear measurement settings that are difficult for existing diffusion-based recovery methods, particularly when the link function relating a signal to its measurements is unknown or discontinuous. It focuses on semi-parametric single index models, a family encompassing several such nonlinear problems.

The proposed reconstruction method requires one round of unconditional diffusion-model sampling and partial inversion. This design keeps the use of the diffusion model compact while applying its learned signal distribution to recovery. The paper establishes theoretical effectiveness under appropriate conditions, so its analytical guarantees are conditional rather than a claim that arbitrary nonlinear measurements can always be inverted accurately.

Experiments use image datasets with different nonlinear measurement models. Compared with competing methods, the approach can produce more accurate reconstructions while requiring significantly fewer neural function evaluations. The result connects reconstruction quality with computational economy: the reported improvements arise in a method designed to use the diffusion model sparingly, including in settings with challenging link functions.
icml-2025-learning-single-index-models-w.tldr: A diffusion-prior recovery method handles single index models with unknown or discontinuous links using one sampling round and partial inversion.

paragraphs: Finding relevant information inside a long input does not automatically produce a good response. The paper focuses on this gap in long-context models, whose generations can remain misaligned or contain hallucinations despite locating salient tokens. LOGO addresses generation quality through preference optimization tailored to long-context alignment.

Long sequences create GPU memory pressure during training. LOGO uses a reference-free preference optimization strategy and a position synthesis method for constructing training data to address this constraint. Its contribution combines an alignment objective with a training approach intended to make that objective practical for long inputs. The focus is on improving how the model generates from its context.

The reported training run uses 0.3B data and takes 16 hours on one machine with eight A800 GPUs. The resulting Llama-3-8B-Instruct-80K model achieves performance comparable to GPT-4 on the reported real-world long-context tasks while preserving capabilities such as language modeling and MMLU performance. The authors also report that LOGO can enlarge the context window while improving generation, connecting context extension with better use of that context.
icml-2025-logo-long-context-alignment-vi.tldr: LOGO makes preference optimization practical for long-context models and improves generation while preserving other evaluated capabilities.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning requires an agent to remain able to adapt as tasks, environments, or data distributions change. That adaptability is called plasticity. This paper studies its deterioration through churn: changes in network outputs induced by the examples in each training batch. The investigation connects increasing output variability with the loss of continued learning ability.

The authors show that plasticity loss is accompanied by worsening churn as the Neural Tangent Kernel matrix gradually loses rank. They also show that reducing churn helps prevent rank collapse and adaptively adjusts the step size of ordinary reinforcement-learning gradients. This provides both a structural connection to the network's learning dynamics and a mechanism for influencing its updates.

The proposed method, Continual Churn Approximated Reduction, or C-CHAIN, puts this perspective into an algorithm. Experiments report better learning performance than baselines across continual-learning environments from OpenAI Gym Control, ProcGen, DeepMind Control Suite, and MinAtar. The findings support churn reduction as a practical way to mitigate plasticity loss across the tested environments.
icml-2025-mitigating-plasticity-loss-in-.tldr: C-CHAIN reduces training-induced output churn to help preserve plasticity and improve continual reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Auction-based federated learning lets a data consumer recruit data owners through bidding. Existing strategies commonly assume the full team must be assembled before training begins. This paper instead considers recruitment across multiple training sessions, where the consumer can begin training and acquire more participants over time. That creates a budget-allocation problem spanning both current and future sessions.

MBOS-AFL uses hierarchical reinforcement learning to coordinate two decisions: how to pace spending between sessions and how to bid within each session. It jointly optimizes these decisions to maximize total utility. The hierarchy links the broader allocation of a finite budget to the individual auction decisions that determine which data are acquired.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets compare the method with seven state-of-the-art approaches. Relative to the best baseline, the authors report average gains of 12.28% in utility, 14.52% in data acquired for a given budget, and 1.23% in resulting model test accuracy. These findings support treating recruitment and spending as a sequence of connected decisions when federated training occurs across multiple sessions.
icml-2025-multi-session-budget-optimizat.tldr: MBOS-AFL coordinates budget pacing and auction bids across federated-learning sessions, improving reported utility, data acquisition, and model accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies training language models for the way their outputs will actually be used at inference time. Its focus is on procedures that draw multiple samples, so the relevant outcome depends on a collection of responses. The central question is whether explicitly optimizing that collection-level objective during training improves the eventual inference procedure.

The authors consider general objectives involving k samples, with particular attention to pass@k and majority voting. Pass@k concerns finding a successful response among the samples, while majority voting uses agreement among responses to choose an answer. These objectives evaluate sampled outputs differently, making the choice of training target consequential for the inference algorithm that follows.

Training on reasoning datasets demonstrates a performance trade-off enabled by these objectives. On code generation tasks, the approach significantly improves pass@k compared with the baseline method. The findings support matching training to a planned inference procedure and its success criterion. They also frame the improvement in terms of the selected objective: the paper reports trade-offs, rather than presenting one training objective as uniformly best for every use of multiple samples.
icml-2025-optimizing-language-models-for.tldr: Training language models for multi-sample inference objectives exposes performance trade-offs and improves reported code-generation pass@k.

paragraphs: PepTune generates peptide structures represented as SMILES strings while optimizing several therapeutic properties together. It builds on masked discrete diffusion, in which generation operates over discrete sequences. A bond-dependent masking schedule and a loss for invalid outputs are designed to ensure that generated sequences describe valid peptide structures.

Its guidance method, Monte Carlo Tree Guidance, operates during inference. It combines classifier-based rewards with expansion of a search tree, balancing exploration of possibilities with refinement of promising sequences. The search targets Pareto-optimal sequences, reflecting the trade-offs that arise when several properties matter simultaneously. The authors present this approach as addressing challenges from gradient estimation and sparse data.

The reported results include diverse, chemically modified peptides optimized jointly for properties such as target binding affinity, membrane permeability, solubility, hemolysis, and non-fouling across disease-relevant targets. The contribution is a generation-and-search framework that can pursue multiple objectives within a discrete design space. The findings support the authors' broader claim that tree-guided masked diffusion offers a modular approach to multi-objective sequence design.
icml-2025-peptune-de-novo-generation-of-.tldr: PepTune combines peptide-aware discrete diffusion with tree-search guidance to generate chemically modified peptides optimized for multiple therapeutic properties.

paragraphs: Autoregressive text generation produces a response token by token without a built-in opportunity to revise earlier choices. This paper studies the consequences using a specific definition of optimality: the joint probability of the complete response, compared with the highest-probability response of the same length. Its theoretical analysis characterizes how the generated sequence can depart from that optimum.

The analysis suggests that noticeable uncertainty during generation may indicate problems in the preceding generation history. Reflection-Window Decoding responds with a sliding window for revisiting text and a criterion for pausing generation. These mechanisms allow the model to alternate between continuing the response and refining content as decoding proceeds.

Selective refinement is intended to balance computational efficiency with the sequence-level objective. The authors report extensive experiments supporting the approach's effectiveness. The key contribution is a decoding framework that makes revision part of generation and uses uncertainty as a possible signal for when revision is useful. The stated optimality concerns response probability, and the uncertainty signal indicates potential suboptimality rather than proving that earlier text is wrong.
icml-2025-reflection-window-decoding-tex.tldr: Reflection-Window Decoding selectively pauses and revises generated text to balance efficiency with whole-response probability.

paragraphs: Robust offline reinforcement learning seeks policies that tolerate changes in environment dynamics while learning from previously collected data. Regularizing transition dynamics can support robustness, but unstructured regularization may lead to overly conservative policies by considering unrealistic transitions. This paper introduces a framework that places latent structure in both the transition model and its regularization.

The framework is a d-rectangular linear Robust Regularized Markov Decision Process. Its proposed algorithm, Robust Regularized Pessimistic Value Iteration, uses linear function approximation and f-divergence regularization of transition kernels. Learning uses a dataset collected in the nominal environment, while the policy objective accounts for admissible changes to that environment's dynamics.

The authors derive instance-dependent upper bounds on policy suboptimality. Those bounds depend on how well the dataset covers state-action pairs visited by the optimal robust policy under robustly admissible transitions. Information-theoretic lower bounds establish near-optimality of the algorithm. Numerical experiments also report robust policies and better computational efficiency than baselines, connecting the structured formulation to both theoretical performance and practical computation.
icml-2025-robust-offline-reinforcement-l.tldr: R2PVI learns robust offline policies using structured transition regularization, with near-optimal guarantees that depend on dataset coverage.

paragraphs: When a graph is divided among federated-learning clients, the split changes how information can propagate. This paper examines two consequences. Spatially, disconnected edges between clients interrupt label signals and weaken the global model's semantic knowledge. Spectrally, differences in signal frequencies across subgraphs encourage local models to specialize in their own propagation patterns.

The authors call the latter effect spectral client drift: local graph neural networks become inconsistent in ways that undermine global generalization. Their S²FGL framework pairs two responses to these problems. A global knowledge repository helps compensate for disrupted label information, while frequency alignment addresses differences in spectral behavior across clients.

Experiments on multiple datasets report superior performance for the combined framework. The paper's contribution is to treat federated graph learning as a problem involving both graph structure and the signals moving over it. Its two mechanisms correspond to distinct consequences of partitioning the graph, and the reported findings support addressing semantic disruption and spectral mismatch together when training a shared graph model.
icml-2025-s-2-fgl-spatial-spectral-feder.tldr: S²FGL combines shared semantic knowledge with frequency alignment to address two forms of information disruption in federated graph learning.

paragraphs: Sampling molecular states at thermodynamic equilibrium requires producing configurations with the right target distribution. Boltzmann generators approach this through normalizing flows and importance sampling. Sequential Boltzmann Generators extend that framework with a faster flow architecture and a more elaborate inference procedure, aiming to make harder molecular systems tractable.

The flow uses a Transformer and works directly with all-atom Cartesian coordinates. Its architecture is exactly invertible and non-equivariant, providing efficient sample generation and likelihood evaluation. That efficiency makes room for additional work during inference. A continuous-time sequential Monte Carlo procedure transports flow-generated samples toward the target distribution using annealed Langevin dynamics.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated metrics on peptide systems. They also report the first equilibrium sampling in Cartesian coordinates for tri-, tetra-, and hexa-peptides that previous Boltzmann generators could not handle. The result illustrates how cheaper generation and likelihood computation can support stronger downstream sampling procedures, expanding the molecular systems accessible within this framework.
icml-2025-scalable-equilibrium-sampling-.tldr: Sequential Boltzmann Generators combine an efficient invertible Transformer flow with sequential Monte Carlo to scale equilibrium sampling of peptides.

paragraphs: Language models running on resource-constrained devices need efficient inference, including in applications motivated by privacy. Spiking neural networks offer a possible route to lower energy use, but familiar Transformer operations can be difficult to implement on neuromorphic hardware. Sorbet focuses on two such obstacles: softmax and layer normalization.

The model introduces PTsoftmax, a shifting-based softmax operation, and BitShifting-based PowerNorm as replacements for the corresponding energy-intensive components. These changes make its Transformer-based spiking architecture more compatible with neuromorphic hardware. Knowledge distillation and quantization then produce a highly compressed model with binary weights, combining architectural changes with model compression.

The authors evaluate Sorbet on GLUE and through ablation studies. They report competitive performance and 27.16-fold energy savings compared with BERT. The findings support the potential of this design for energy-efficient language-model inference. Its contribution is to address difficult operations inside the Transformer alongside compression, connecting hardware compatibility to the model's internal computation rather than relying only on reduced model size.
icml-2025-sorbet-a-neuromorphic-hardware.tldr: Sorbet replaces difficult Transformer operations with shifting-based alternatives and compresses a spiking language model, reporting 27.16-fold energy savings over BERT.

paragraphs: Generating useful synthetic text under differential privacy can be computationally demanding when the generator is a billion-parameter language model. Prompt-based alternatives introduce dependence on manual prompts and can use private information inefficiently. CTCL addresses these issues with a smaller conditional generator and a separate model of the private data's topic distribution.

The framework first trains a 140-million-parameter generator and a clustering-based topic model on public data. It then adapts the generator through differentially private finetuning to capture fine-grained textual information. Separately, the topic model extracts a differentially private histogram describing distributional information. Synthetic examples are produced by sampling from the generator according to that histogram.

This division gives the framework two complementary sources of private-domain adaptation: the generator learns textual details, while the histogram determines the mixture of topics to sample. Evaluation across five domains reports effectiveness, particularly under strong privacy requirements. Ablation studies support the individual components and highlight scalability. The approach still uses private finetuning, but applies it to a lightweight generator rather than a billion-scale model.
icml-2025-synthesizing-privacy-preservin.tldr: CTCL combines a small privately finetuned generator with a private topic histogram to synthesize text without tuning a billion-scale model.

paragraphs: Offline black-box optimization uses existing task data to seek good solutions. A major obstacle to sharing an optimizer across tasks is that numerical search spaces differ in structure and dimensionality. This paper investigates whether language-model representations can provide a common space for these heterogeneous problems, helping optimization move beyond separate fixed-dimensional task settings.

The authors explore multiple approaches, including end-to-end next-token prediction and learning latent spaces with strong representational capabilities. Both directions use language models as a route to shared representations, with particular attention to string embedding spaces. For training, they collect optimization tasks and offline data from open-source academic work.

Experiments demonstrate cross-task applicability and effectiveness of the proposed approaches. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that combining language-model priors with learned string embeddings can overcome traditional representational barriers. The contribution is a promising direction toward general-purpose offline optimization: a shared representation makes heterogeneous tasks more amenable to common learning methods, with the reported experiments supporting that direction.
icml-2025-towards-universal-offline-blac.tldr: The paper explores language-model priors and string embeddings as shared representations for offline black-box optimization across heterogeneous tasks.

paragraphs: Different pretrained vision-language models have different strengths, making the choice of model consequential for a downstream task. Evaluating every available candidate can exceed the available time or data. Model Label Learning addresses this selection problem by giving models reusable descriptions of their specialties and utility, then matching those descriptions to a task's requirements.

The framework has three stages. Model labeling characterizes candidate models; model selection uses those labels to identify suitable candidates; model reuse combines selected models in an ensemble for the target task. Labeling is performed independently of the target task, so the characterization work can be reused. The framework can also grow as additional candidate models become available.

The authors introduce a benchmark containing 49 vision-language models and 17 target-task datasets, and report experiments supporting effective selection and reuse. The approach connects efficient model discovery with ensemble-based adaptation. Its practical significance is that choosing among pretrained models becomes a structured matching process, supported by reusable model information rather than requiring a fresh evaluation of every candidate for every task.
icml-2025-vision-language-model-selectio.tldr: Model Label Learning characterizes vision-language models once, matches them to downstream tasks, and reuses selected models through ensembles.

paragraphs: Evaluating image watermarks involves more than measuring pixel differences. The paper argues that established statistical metrics can miss watermark visibility and damage to image meaning, while also requiring an original image that may be unavailable. WMarkGPT addresses assessment directly from the watermarked image, without access to its unwatermarked counterpart.

The multimodal language model predicts watermark visibility and produces descriptions of watermark location, content, and effects on image semantics. To develop these abilities, the authors construct three visual question-answering datasets covering object locations, synthetic watermarking, and real watermarking. A three-stage learning pipeline progressively trains the model to handle precise spatial descriptions and images with varied content.

Experiments on synthetic and real watermarking question-answering datasets show WMarkGPT outperforming existing multimodal language models, with significant improvements in visibility prediction and content description. The contribution expands assessment from a statistical score to an explanation of what a watermark does to the image. Its reference-free design is especially relevant when the original image is unavailable, while its textual outputs address effects on content as well as visual appearance.
icml-2025-wmarkgpt-watermarked-image-und.tldr: WMarkGPT assesses watermark visibility, location, content, and semantic impact from watermarked images without needing the originals.
